title: Everyday routines and habits
aim: Explain a working day, compare two people’s commitments, check assumptions and account for a change of routine.
entry: A1 4.5–4.8: sequenced morning actions, home tasks and Do you...? exchanges; these are supporting knowledge, not the opening curriculum again.
A1 4.9–4.10: weekdays, day parts and whole-hour times. A1 6.12: transport departure/arrival questions with does.
A1 3.3: present actions; A1 5.6: wants/needs; A1 6.11: goes; A1 7.7–7.8: invitation, refusal, alternative and audible repair.
exit: Explain departure, start, finish and return times in a connected account.
Report another person’s schedule accurately, contrast two schedules and resolve a mistaken assumption.
Use frequency, intervals, places and reasons to establish whether an arrangement fits the stated facts.
Distinguish a usual routine from today’s explicit exception and update a practical decision.
Distinguish familiar broad routines from more precise daily actions and follow an explicitly stated preparation sequence.
boundaries: Whole hours only; precise minutes and dates remain Unit 3. No past tense before Unit 5.
The first lesson adds useful daily-life chunks and a purposeful exchange. A1 verbs are support, not new Learn targets.
A complete conversation may exceed eight words. Only each Use tile construction retains its current 2–8-word boundary; a short construction is one component of the larger task.
No automatic placement gate, new free-conversation assessment, scheduler or routine-calendar UI is assumed. Spanish support and the existing five stages remain.

Teach one useful meaning of each multiword action. Put off means postpone, introduced in Unit 3; it is not the opposite of put on. Particle-object rearrangement and new irregular past are not inferred from this unit.

lessons.title: A day with real commitments
lessons.outcome: Find out when a person leaves, starts and finishes work, then use the answer to choose a workable meeting time.
newTargets: leave home
start work
finish work
arrive home
meet / Let’s meet at... as a new meeting action within the inherited invitation frame
What time do you...? applied to a person’s commitments
lessons.a1Baseline: A1 already asks Do you work?, sequences a school morning and asks a transport departure time. It does not establish these four personal-schedule chunks or a productive interview about them.
lessons.progression: Four useful schedule chunks plus meet support a two-person exchange and a decision using two facts. The learner goes beyond identifying an action or attaching every day to it.
lessons.task: Hear two people’s different work/return times, ask for the missing return time, and select the meeting option compatible with the complete account. A person finishing work at five is not assumed to be home at five.
lessons.load: One new communicative focus: finding out about a daily schedule. Introduce the four chunks in chronological pairs, then the question using an already-modeled chunk. Keep I/you, whole hours and familiar locations; third-person forms, frequency, intervals and reasons wait. Explicitly teach meet in the closing Let’s meet at... proposal. Pilot this sequence rather than presenting the actions, question and proposal together on the first card.
prerequisites: A1 work, home, I/you, at, whole hours and explicit day-period context
A1 question/reply turn taking and Please repeat
lessons.story: Ana and Luis discuss a weekday visit. Ana describes leaving and starting work, then finishing and arriving home. Luis asks for the missing time; he must distinguish end of work from arrival home before choosing between two meeting times. A second encounter changes the facts, not only the character picture. Spanish setup establishes that both people already want to meet at home after both return, and the final invitation receives an explicit OK. Home arrival alone does not prove availability or willingness. Supply morning/evening context for every stated time; no commuting duration is inferred.
models: I leave home at seven. I start work at eight.
What time do you finish work?
I finish work at five. I arrive home at six.
What time do you arrive home?
I arrive home at six. Let’s meet at seven.

stages.Learn: Introduce leave home/start work with the same person and two successive scenes; then finish work/arrive home with the matching return journey. Teach What time do you...? beside its specific reply. The connected final model brings those four events together; it is not four isolated verb-label cards. Before the closing proposal, explicitly introduce meet inside Let’s meet at seven.
stages.Recognize: Match a written event-and-time statement to the correct point in a clearly ordered day. Keep finish-work and get-home images distinct. Written recognition can isolate one meaning at a time while the surrounding sequence preserves the practical goal.
stages.Listen: Hear a short connected account with two relevant times before choosing a proposed meeting option. A follow-up supplies the previously missing return time. Keep the answer-bearing time out of the initial scene and distinguish a correct fact from a usable arrangement.
stages.Speak: Practice the questioner and respondent in adjacent turns. Include the two-sentence finish/return answer as a meaningful spoken model, with existing replay and feedback. The response is longer because both facts matter, not to meet a word quota.
stages.Use: Construct What time do you finish work? then I finish work at five. and I arrive home at six. as adjacent complete components of the exchange. Each construction stays within 2–8 words, with the existing guided-first allocation.

lessons.pronunciation: Phrase grouping in leave home and arrive home; clear start/finish and final consonants in the complete utterance. Do not require native-like speed.
lessons.evidence: On a fresh exchange the learner selects an arrangement consistent with both the finish and return time and distinguishes which question obtains the missing fact. Model repetition and tile construction remain supported production, not evidence of spontaneous negotiation.
lessons.repair: Replay the relevant pair of events after a finish/arrival confusion; explain the distinction in Spanish without replaying the whole lesson. Existing A1 time difficulty links to targeted support rather than restarting clock teaching.
retrieval: 1.2 reports the same four actions with another subject; 1.3 adds an interval; 1.7 checks assumptions.
1.11 review and 1.12 mission require a compatible arrangement; Unit 4 transfers the chunks to work responsibilities.
lessons.media: Use ordered, clearly differentiated leaving/work/return states in existing image slots. A clock or timetable shown before Listen must not reveal the assessed time. No interactive planner or inferred travel duration. Establish the agreed-visit condition without revealing the answer, and make a.m./p.m. or day-period context consistent across all chronological views.

Moves start/finish from v1 Unit 4 into a more substantial opening. Adds leave home/arrive home as contextual chunks.

lessons.title: Two people, different days
lessons.outcome: Report two people’s commitments and explain the contrast that matters for a shared plan.
newTargets: leaves
starts
finishes
arrives home
works as the selected third-person form of known work
but connecting contrasting facts
lessons.a1Baseline: A1 already contains he has, she needs, he wants and goes. Third-person meaning is familiar, but the four new schedule inflections are not automatically known.
lessons.progression: Extend a productive system in service of reporting another speaker’s information. A contrast changes who can participate; a third-person ending is not the lesson’s whole purpose.
lessons.task: Listen to each person’s first-person account, then identify and correct a report that assigns one person’s finish or return time to the other.
lessons.load: The base chunks are secure from 1.1. Teach selected third-person forms inside chronological pairs; introduce but only after each contrasting fact is understood. No new jobs, travel vocabulary, negatives or interrogative forms.
prerequisites: 1.1 schedule chunks and personal time questions
A1 names, he/she, and; known goes is support
lessons.story: Ana starts and finishes earlier than Luis. A host preparing a visit receives their separate reports and mixes up one time. The learner matches the correct person-to-event facts and gives a contrast needed to settle the visit. A separate, explicitly introduced encounter contrasts Ana leaving home with Luis arriving home; do not assign this opposite schedule to their earlier encounter.
models: Ana starts work at eight, but Luis starts work at nine.
She finishes work at five. He finishes work at six.
Ana arrives home at six, but Luis arrives home at seven.
Luis leaves home at eight. He arrives home at seven.

stages.Learn: Model I start work... beside Ana starts work... in one reporting encounter, then do the same for the remaining chunks. After two statements have established differing facts, model the complete contrast with but. Explicitly model I work... / Ana works... before later interval reports use works.
stages.Recognize: Match complete person/event/time statements to distinct factual records. Contrasts need evidence for both clauses; do not use the same generic work photo to test all four actions.
stages.Listen: Hear two first-person accounts and choose the accurate third-person report. Include one plausible swap of the people’s times. After correction, select the usable meeting option.
stages.Speak: Practice a two-sentence report and one connected contrast. Keep each person’s referent clear; longer models use meaningful phrase groups and the existing recording/replay path.
stages.Use: Build Ana starts work at eight. and Luis starts work at nine. as adjacent complete report components. After an explicitly established contrasting departure/return scene, construct Ana leaves home, but Luis arrives home. as a complete bounded contrast. Longer two-time reports stay in Listen and Speak.

lessons.pronunciation: Natural /s/, /z/ and the extra syllable in finishes; audible but within an intelligible contrast.
lessons.evidence: A fresh report correctly tracks person, event and time. Recognition establishes referent comprehension; supplied tiles do not prove independent verb agreement.
lessons.repair: If the person is confused, return to that person’s statement. If the verb form is confused, show the already-taught first/third-person pair; do not mix both error explanations.
retrieval: 1.3 interval reports and 1.6 frequency reports reuse the selected forms.
1.7 checks assumptions about them; 1.11–1.12 require correct reports.
lessons.media: Distinct speakers, matching voices and two full contextual accounts. A color or clothing shortcut must not substitute for listening to the assigned facts.

lessons.title: Which time actually works?
lessons.outcome: Use a work interval and explicit before/after relationships to select a workable time and distinguish the order events happen from the order they are mentioned.
newTargets: from...to... for a time interval
before/after + familiar event noun: before dinner / after work
bounded clause bridge: before/after + I + known present verb, as in before I start work / after I finish work
lessons.a1Baseline: A1 tells whole-hour times and sequences a school morning with first/then. A1+ 1.1–1.2 establishes start, finish, departure and return events. Neither that sequence nor knowing before/after + noun automatically establishes a before/after clause.
lessons.progression: Move from two separate event times to an interval, then from a familiar event label to a complete event clause. Interpret the temporal relationship even when the later event is mentioned first, then apply it to the agreed visit.
lessons.task: First identify the same two-event order in two differently worded reports; then select a meeting time consistent with the supplied work interval and dinner constraint. A correct time label is insufficient if the proposed time conflicts with either stated commitment.
lessons.load: Three explicit steps, each checked before adding the next: start/end facts → from...to... interval; before/after + familiar event noun; before/after + I + an already-known present verb. The final bridge uses only leave home/start work/finish work/arrive home, not new daily-action vocabulary. Keep one day, whole hours and two events per comparison. Clause-fronting, before/after + -ing, new question forms, frequency and date arithmetic are outside this lesson. Do not present all three forms in the opening account; the later constraint task combines only already-grounded relations.
prerequisites: 1.1–1.2 leave/start/finish/arrive home and event-time reports
A1 first/then, whole hours and known work/lunch/dinner
lessons.story: Ana and Luis already want to arrange a visit after work. Establish work start/finish and a separate return event. The learner interprets the same chronological pair in before and after reports, then hears the dinner constraint needed to choose between two visit times. Both people explicitly agree to the accepted proposal; presence at home never establishes willingness and no commuting duration is inferred.
models: I start work at eight. I finish work at five.
I work from eight to five.
Let’s meet after work.
I arrive home before dinner.
I leave home before I start work.
I finish work before I arrive home.
I arrive home after I finish work.
Ana works from eight to five. She arrives home at six.

stages.Learn: Step 1: model two endpoint facts, then I work from eight to five. Step 2: model before dinner and after work against already-established events. Step 3: explicitly model I leave home before I start work. Pair I finish work before I arrive home. with I arrive home after I finish work. and ground their identical event order. The clause bridge is a declared new structure, not incidental wording. Keep subject I in the bridge.
stages.Recognize: Match complete written interval and noun-phrase relations to factual evidence, then match the taught before/after clause pair to the same ordered two-event sequence. Include a reversed-event alternative only when unambiguously false. Separate relation comprehension from clock reading.
stages.Listen: After the clause models, hear I arrive home after I finish work. and identify the finish-work event as earlier even though arrive home is heard first. In a fresh paired encounter, contrast before with after while keeping the two familiar events unchanged. Then use an explicit work interval and dinner constraint to choose a usable proposal. Do not reveal the listening order through an already-labelled picture.
stages.Speak: Rehearse the interval and after-work proposal, then both equivalent before/after clause reports with clear phrase groups. The same events can be mentioned in a different order without changing the timeline. Production remains modeled; do not infer spontaneous clause formation.
stages.Use: Build I work from eight to five. and Let’s meet after work. After explicit clause teaching, construct I leave home before I start work. and I arrive home after I finish work. as complete seven-word targets. Keep the guided-first allocation; do not split a subordinate clause into a fragment tile task.

lessons.pronunciation: Keep from/to and before/after intelligible within complete phrases; phrase grouping must not make the first-mentioned event sound automatically first in time.
lessons.evidence: On a fresh pair of familiar events, identify the earlier event from both before and after reports, including a report that mentions the later event first. Separately select a meeting time respecting both supplied commitments. Record whether replay or the visual sequence was needed; no assumed commute or free-production claim.
lessons.repair: If the learner follows mention order, isolate the two events and contrast the explicitly taught equivalent reports, with concise Spanish support. If interval endpoints are confused, repair that distinction separately. Return to the combined decision only after the specific relation is understood.
retrieval: 1.4 first grounds each new action with first/then, then retrieves the taught clause bridge with before I leave home / after I arrive home.
1.8 interviews and 1.9 reasons reuse noun-phrase relations; 1.11 reviews interval, noun and clause forms; 1.12 uses a before-clause preparation cue in the agreed-visit story.
Unit 3 appointment options and Unit 4 opening/work hours use the interval and explicit event order.
lessons.media: A complete pictorial sequence must fit the supported still-image pattern; no new calendar interaction. Spanish context can establish the visual convention but cannot disclose the answer.

lessons.title: Get ready, leave on time, arrive home
lessons.outcome: Explain a practical getting-ready sequence and distinguish waking, leaving bed, dressing and removing clothes in a day with stated commitments.
newTargets: get up = leave bed, contrasted with known wake up
take a shower = wash under a shower
put on + clothing = dress in that item
take off + clothing = remove that item
go to bed = go/get into bed to sleep, not necessarily fall asleep
lessons.a1Baseline: A1 4.5 already teaches wake up, wash my face, brush my teeth, eat breakfast and get dressed; A1 7.3 supplies clothing. Naming those morning actions again would restart the course. These five meanings are missing from the declared A1 inventory.
lessons.progression: Use more precise daily actions in a familiar sequence, contrast states that previously shared a broad label, and identify a wrong step in a plan for a stated departure. This adds useful lexical range while grammar stays familiar.
lessons.task: Follow one person getting ready for a stated morning departure and returning in the evening. Correct a report that equates waking with getting up or puts clothing removal before departure when the stated plan says otherwise. Select the account consistent with the explicit sequence, not assumptions about hygiene or clothing customs.
lessons.load: Five related action meanings in two clear episodes: first wake up/get up and take a shower; then put on/take off using known shoes or jacket; finally go to bed in the evening. Ground every action in a complete I statement and connect the first practice with familiar first/then. Only after those meanings are understood, retrieve 1.3’s already-modeled before/after + I + known verb bridge with before I leave home / after I arrive home. Do not introduce third-person inflections, particle movement, pronoun objects or past forms. Clause retrieval is a later pass through grounded actions, not an additional first-exposure demand.
prerequisites: A1 4.5–4.7 morning actions, clothes, open/close and simple present I/you
A1 7.3–7.5 known jacket/shoes and weather context
A1+ 1.1 commitments and 1.3 before/after + event noun, then explicitly modeled before/after + I + known present verb
lessons.story: Ana has agreed to leave home at eight. Her spoken plan says she wakes at six, gets up at seven, takes a shower and puts on her shoes before leaving. A clearly marked evening episode shows taking off those shoes at home and going to bed. Explicit times/context define the facts; the plan does not judge a learner’s personal routine.
models: I wake up at six. I get up at seven.

newTargets: Why...? in the bounded Why not? and Why do/does...? frames

lessons.story: A visit at five is declined because work finishes at six. The alternative at seven resolves that stated obstacle. Let’s meet at seven. OK.

Why do you put on your jacket? Because it is cold.
Why do you take off your jacket? Because it is hot.

Longer reasons remain in listening and speaking; do not make fragment tiles. A supplied tile bank remains supported construction.

lessons.progression: Transfer the unit’s tools to new combinations and identify the relevant follow-up without a new-language load.
lessons.task: Across three bounded encounters, establish a work/return schedule, correct a mistaken report and revise one arrangement after an explicit exception.
lessons.load: No new assessed language. Spread the frequency forms and question types across separate encounters; no single scene requires every target. The review covers the full retained inventory on successful paths.
prerequisites: 1.1–1.10 complete target map
lessons.story: Fresh people and facts: a workday visit, a study-place interview and a corrected home-arrival plan. Each encounter has one practical resolution; they are clearly separated rather than pretending to be one overloaded conversation.
models: What time does she finish work? She finishes at six, but she arrives home at seven.

I finish work before I arrive home. I arrive home after I finish work.

lessons.title: Mission: make the visit work
lessons.outcome: Clarify the needed schedule and routine facts, correct an assumption and use today’s update to agree a workable visit.
lessons.a1Baseline: A1 already completes a social outing. This mission requires reconciling several people’s commitments and a revision, using the new Unit 1 language.

lessons.task: Establish Ana and Luis’s schedules, obtain the missing return time, correct one swapped fact, clarify how often Ana studies at home before hearing today’s changed study place and confirm a visit that respects both people’s stated constraints. One getting-ready beat requires the correct put-on step before the agreed departure, after the schedule and willingness are established.
lessons.load: One goal, two principal people and one meaningful update. Do not add travel purchases, calendar dates or a third problem to increase apparent difficulty. The mission samples frequency vocabulary naturally; the review carries full form coverage.
prerequisites: 1.1–1.11; A1 familiar invitation and repair tools
lessons.story: The learner helps arrange a visit after work. Each chapter supplies only information needed for the next choice. The final scene shows the people arriving at the agreed known place and time, with no new English. Explicit setup establishes that both people want the visit after their commitments. The final revised time/place receives an invitation and a spoken OK; neither a work finish nor a location photograph proves consent or availability. Do not infer an unprovided travel duration. Before the current-place update, the learner knows Ana studies at home but not how often. Ask her the taught How often do you study at home? and retain usually in the report; then the explicit today update requires checking the current place. The frequency answer supplies a routine baseline, not permission to infer today’s location or availability.
models: She finishes work at six, but she arrives home at seven.
Does Luis work on Saturday? No, he doesn’t.
How often do you study at home? I usually study at home.
Ana usually studies at home, but today she is studying at the library.

She arrives home at seven. Let’s meet at eight. OK.
Why not? Because she works from eight to six.
I put on my shoes before I leave home.

stages.Continuous story: Chapter1 establishes the two schedules. Chapter2 obtains a missing fact and corrects one assumption. Chapter3 first clarifies missing frequency with a brief known-place interview, then introduces the current location update. Chapter4 confirms the agreed visit, completes the meaningful getting-ready step and shows arrival. No extra bedtime episode and no five-stage mission menu.
stages.Listening decisions: Require the learner to use the full supplied fact set, including the last correction. Spoken information must be necessary, with visible targets genuinely distinguishing the candidates. The practical visit includes a preparation beat that distinguishes put on shoes from take off shoes; it advances the same visit rather than adding an unrelated bedtime story. After the action is grounded, the successful preparation cue uses I put on my shoes before I leave home.; the correct sequence must respect the clause. A brief known-place/unknown-frequency encounter requires How often do you study at home? and an accurate usually report before the current-place update; it retrieves the 1.6 interview function and studies. The successful response must preserve usually rather than overstate always, and then act on today’s explicit update. No new grammar or separate subplot is added.
stages.Voice gates: Use existing question-view/response-view supported gates for a schedule answer, a correction and a connected reason/confirmation where supported. These rehearse production; they are not spontaneous speech tests.
